name: Kira Garcia

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Kira, thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for any AI company, employer, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on a council housing job on Mill Lane, forty new flats for families off the waiting list. I'm there by seven, I carry timber, cut noggins, fix stud walls with Patrice, who's twenty-two and honestly better than me at most of it. I came to this late, after the hospital laundry where I worked for thirty years shut, so at fifty-eight I'm still the one asking how to set out a door lining. My knees hate the stairs, but I like seeing a wall stand up that wasn't there in the morning.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What wears you out most, and what keeps you going?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The cold wears me out, and the new timesheet app they made us put on our phones, which I can't make work, so Declan the foreman does it for me and sighs. What keeps me going is the people, and that these flats are for real families, not investors. My partner Tomás cleans buses part-time and his lungs are bad, so my wage is most of what we live on. We rent, and we've got maybe two weeks of money put by, if that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, to be honest. At break I'd tell the crew it was always going to be a toy for office people, and online I'd share something about how the money should have gone on housing instead. I'm in the union, so I'd probably say that in the branch meeting too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it means my life stays as hard as it already is. AI going quiet doesn't pay my rent or fix my knees. I'd still be the oldest improver on the site, earning less than the young ones, and still one bad winter from being behind on bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on, same as now, and keep paying my union subs because that's what actually got us the pay rise last year. I'd keep trying to pass my carpentry level one course at the college on Tuesday nights, even though I failed the written bit once. Nothing about AI would change my plans, because I don't have room for plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relieved, a bit, that I don't have to learn yet another thing I don't understand. But there's still that knot in my stomach every time the rent goes out, and that's nothing to do with computers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said nothing would change. Is there anything about this picture that would still bother you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The timesheet app, and things like it. Even if AI is hype, the bosses will still use these little apps to watch us, count our minutes, tell us we were four minutes late back from tea. That's the bit of it I'd see, not robots, just more watching.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you think gains if things carry on like this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The people who own the big building firms, same as always. Prices go up, the flats get sold to investors, and the likes of me carry the boards up the stairs. Hype or no hype, that part doesn't change.

S0.say: I'd say I always knew it was a toy for office people and the money should have gone into housing. I'd say it at break, online and at my union branch meeting.
S0.think: Privately I think nothing gets easier for me, because AI was never what was making my life hard. I'd still be the oldest improver on site, earning the least, one bad winter from falling behind.
S0.do: Carries on at the Mill Lane site and keeps paying union subs. Keeps retaking her carpentry level one course on Tuesday nights at the college, with no other changes planned.
S0.feel: A small relief at not having to learn something new, sitting on top of the same old worry about rent.
S0.quote: Even if AI is hype, the bosses will still use these little apps to watch us, count our minutes, tell us we were four minutes late back from tea.
S0.fieldNote: Kira treats AI as a side issue next to rent, knees and low pay. Her one worry here is surveillance through apps, which she already feels with the site timesheet. The union is the only lever she believes in, and she credits it with her last pay rise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly why we need the union strong and the government stepping in. If they're going to change everyone's job, the workers should get a say and the companies should pay for the retraining. I'd say it loud, because nobody else on my site will.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think it means I'm the first to go. I'm slow, I'm old for a learner, and I can't use the apps, so if a site needs fewer hands they'll keep Patrice and let me go. I'm not daft, I can see how the list would look.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push the branch to get something in writing about who goes first if jobs shrink, so it's not just the old and the slow. At home I'd cut the phone contract and the takeaway on Fridays, maybe sixty a month saved. I'd ask the college if there's a course that's more hands than screen, like dry stone walling or restoration, where they still want people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tight in the chest. I've been here before, with the laundry, when they brought in the big machines across town and we all knew before they told us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happened at the laundry, and what did you learn from it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They said for two years it was just new equipment, and then one Friday there was a letter on everyone's locker. The union got us three extra weeks of pay, which was something. What I learned is you start shouting early, because by the time the letter comes it's too late.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you try to learn the new tools this time, even a little?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe the timesheet app, if Patrice sat with me, because I'd have to. But I won't pretend I'd be good at it. I'd rather spend my energy making sure the rules are fair than learning to tap a screen faster than a twenty-year-old.

S1.say: I'd say this is why we need a strong union and the government stepping in. Workers should get a say and companies should pay for retraining.
S1.think: Honestly, I'd be first out, because I'm slow, I'm older and I can't use the apps. I can already picture the list with Patrice kept and my name crossed off.
S1.do: Pushes her union branch for a written agreement on who goes first if jobs shrink. Cuts the phone contract and Friday takeaway to save about sixty a month and asks the college about hands-on courses such as restoration.
S1.feel: Tight in the chest, because it reminds her of the laundry closing.
S1.quote: They said for two years it was just new equipment, and then one Friday there was a letter on everyone's locker.
S1.fieldNote: The laundry closure is her template for every change: slow warnings, then a sudden letter. That makes her act early through the union rather than through retraining on tech. She would rather fight for fair rules than learn the tools, and she's clear about that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a disgrace that a handful of rich men in tech got to decide this for all of us without a single vote. I'd be at whatever protest there was, carrying a sign. And I'd say the government has to pay people a proper income straight away, not in five years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be finished. Two years from now I'm sixty, I've got two weeks of savings, Tomás can't work full-time, and there's no other building work round here even now. If robots are putting up stud walls, I've got nothing else to sell.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First month I'd be at the council and the advice centre finding out every benefit we could get, and I'd tell my daughter Nell we might need to move in with her for a while. I'd stop the car insurance and sell the car, it would fetch about eight hundred. I'd go to every union meeting going, because if there's ever a time for everyone to stand together, that's it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like the floor's gone. I'd be lying awake doing sums that don't add up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Nell when you ask about moving in?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm sorry, love, I always said I'd never be a burden on you. She's got two kids in a two-bed flat, so it'd be me on the sofa and Tomás on a camp bed, and I'd hate every night of it. But I'd say it, because what else is there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With only two years, is there anything at all you'd do differently before it arrives?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really, I'd just hold on harder. Two years isn't time to learn a trade, it's barely time to finish the course I'm failing. I'd work every hour of overtime they'd give me and put it by for the rent before the letters start.

S2.say: I'd say it's a disgrace that a few rich men in tech decided this without a vote. I'd be at the protests and I'd demand the government pays people a proper income straight away.
S2.think: Off the record, I'd be finished: sixty, two weeks of savings, Tomás unable to work full-time and no other building work nearby. If robots can put up stud walls, I've got nothing else to sell.
S2.do: Goes to the council and advice centre in the first month to claim every benefit, sells the car for about eight hundred and asks her daughter about moving in. Attends every union meeting and protest she can.
S2.feel: Like the floor has gone, lying awake doing sums that don't add up.
S2.quote: She's got two kids in a two-bed flat, so it'd be me on the sofa and Tomás on a camp bed, and I'd hate every night of it.
S2.fieldNote: With two years' warning Kira sees no exit at all, and her plans shift straight to survival: benefits, selling the car, moving in with family. Asked what two years would let her do, she said only 'hold on harder'. Her anger at tech owners is real, but under it is shame about leaning on her daughter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years, so there's no excuse this time. I'd tell the branch and anyone online that we need a law now, before it lands, so people over fifty-five can retire early on a decent pension. Five years is enough time to pass a law if they want to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think five years gets me to sixty-three, and that's still short of my pension. So I'd be scared, but less sick to my stomach than with the two-year one. It depends whether those years get used for anything, and I don't trust them to use it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay on Mill Lane and the next site as long as they'd have me, and I'd put twenty a week in the credit union, which is what I can do if we drop the Friday takeaway for good. I'd get the union to campaign for early pension for older trades. And I'd ask Nell and her husband now, not later, whether a move in with them would be possible, so it's not a shock.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, but with a bit of air. Like being told about a storm on Tuesday instead of hearing thunder.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does five years change compared with two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two, I'd be grabbing at anything. With five, I can at least ask for things before the letter comes, which is what I said I learned at the laundry. But I'm still not going to become a robot engineer at sixty, let's be straight about that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Twenty a week over five years is about five thousand. How far does that go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About four months of rent, not a pension. It's something to stop us going under while we wait for the pension, that's all. But four months can be the difference between keeping the flat and losing it, so I'd do it.

S3.say: I'd say five years leaves no excuse and we need a law now so people over fifty-five can retire early on a decent pension. I'd push that through the union and online.
S3.think: Five years only gets me to sixty-three, still short of my pension. I'm scared, but less sick about it than with two years, though I don't trust anyone to use the time well.
S3.do: Stays on the building sites as long as she's kept and puts twenty a week into the credit union by dropping takeaways. Campaigns through the union for early pensions for older trades and raises a possible move with her daughter early.
S3.feel: Scared, with a little room to breathe, like hearing a storm forecast instead of thunder.
S3.quote: With five, I can at least ask for things before the letter comes, which is what I said I learned at the laundry.
S3.fieldNote: Five years doesn't make Kira look for a new career; it gives her time to organise and to warn her family. Her savings plan is small and she knows it; she called five thousand 'four months of rent, not a pension'. She still won't consider learning AI tools, even with time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a real chance to do this fairly, so let's not waste it. I'd want the union and the council to make a plan for every trade, with dates. And I'd say anyone who uses those years just to make more profit should be ashamed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years gets me to sixty-eight, and by then I'd be on my state pension anyway. So it's not me I'd be most frightened for, it's Patrice and the young ones, and Nell's kids. I'd probably just about make it through, if my knees do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and keep doing my college nights, maybe actually pass this time. I'd put the twenty a week away like I said, and push the union for training paid by the companies for the young ones. I wouldn't change much else, I'd just keep my head down and get to the finish line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sad more than scared. It's like watching the tide come in when you're already near the top of the beach.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You're near the top of the beach. Who's still on the sand?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Patrice, for one. He's put three years into an apprenticeship and he's good, he can hang a door in twenty minutes, and in ten years he'd be thirty-two with nothing to show. I'd tell him straight to get his union card and a second skill, because hands alone won't be enough for him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would ten years change anything about how you see the AI tools themselves?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years or a hundred, I'll leave that to the kids. I know that sounds stubborn, and it is. I've got enough on my plate getting down the ladder in the morning without learning to talk to a computer.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is a real chance to do this fairly, so don't waste it. The union and the council should make a plan for every trade, and anyone who just takes the profit should be ashamed.
S4.think: I'd reach my state pension at sixty-eight and just about get through, if my knees hold. My bigger fear is for Patrice, the young ones and Nell's kids.
S4.do: Keeps working and keeps going to her college evening course, aiming to pass. Saves twenty a week and pushes the union for company-paid training for younger workers.
S4.feel: More sad than scared, as if watching the tide come in from near the top of the beach.
S4.quote: It's like watching the tide come in when you're already near the top of the beach.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years shifts Kira's fear away from herself and onto younger workers like Patrice. She still won't touch AI tools; asked directly, she said, 'Ten years or a hundred, I'll leave that to the kids.' She stays anxious because her path to the pension depends on her body and a thin budget.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, no question, because I'd have nothing and no time to get anything. What would help is a proper early pension for people my age in hard jobs, and the union being in the room when they decide who goes first. Not a website, not a course on a screen, an actual person at the council who'll sit with me and Tomás.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about my body. Everyone talks about robots doing the work, but I'm fifty-eight on a building site and some mornings I can barely get down the ladder. The robots would just finish what the stairs started.

headlineQuote: The robots would just finish what the stairs started.
portrait: Kira Garcia is a 58-year-old carpenter's improver on a council housing site, who came into building after thirty years in a hospital laundry that closed. She's a committed union member, never uses AI tools and fights the site's timesheet app. AI hype barely registers next to her rent and knees, but steady change brings back memories of the laundry letters, and fast AGI leaves her imagining life on her daughter's sofa. With five or ten years she shifts to organising for early pensions and worrying about young workers like her friend Patrice.
biggestWorry: The two-year AGI picture worries her most, because she would have no money and no time to find anything else.
whatWouldHelp: A proper early pension for older people in hard jobs, the union in the room when cuts are decided, and a real person at the council to sit down with her and Tomás.
